detail: If no sparse point cloud is available, discretize randomly sampled training rays into 3D samples to estimate scene content distribution, then partition similarly [S1].

The claim states that if no sparse point cloud is available, one should discretize randomly sampled training rays into 3D samples to estimate scene content distribution, then partition similarly. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'In cases where a sparse point cloud is unavailable... we instead discretize randomly sampled training rays into 3D samples. This serves as an estimation of the scene content distribution... enabling us to proceed with partitioning in a similar manner.' The claim is fully supported by the evidence.

[G] The concept of restricting NeRF queries to relevant volumes originated with early observations that uniform sampling wastes computation on empty space. [11379-vaxnerf.md] VaxNeRF introduced the visual hull as a hard constraint. [13537-block-nerf.md] Block-NeRF addressed scalability by decomposing the scene. [9538-zip-nerf-training-procedure.md] Zip-NeRF introduced sparse caching for inverse rendering. [S1] Spatial partitioning for multi-GPU scaling was formalized in NeRF-XL.

The evidence supports the claim regarding NeRF-XL (Source S1) formalizing spatial partitioning for multi-GPU scaling. However, the claim also attributes specific origins and contributions to other papers (VaxNeRF, Block-NeRF, Zip-NeRF) which are not present in the provided evidence text (Source S1). Since the evidence only covers the last part of the claim, the verdict is partial.

A strategy to create tiles that ensures balanced workload (similar number of network evaluations/ray samples) across GPUs, avoiding suboptimal GPU utilization caused by uneven scene content distribution [S1].

The claim accurately reflects the content of Source [S1]. The source explicitly states that the proposed partitioning scheme aims to evenly distribute workload (similar number of ray samples/points) across GPUs to avoid suboptimal GPU utilization caused by uneven distribution. It details the two methods (using a sparse point cloud via CDF or using discretized training rays) and mentions the speed of the process, all of which are present in the claim.
If a sparse point cloud is available, recursively identify the plane where the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) equals 0.5 for the 3D point distribution along each axis to partition space [S1].

The claim states that if a sparse point cloud is available, one should recursively identify the plane where the CDF equals 0.5 for the 3D point distribution along each axis to partition space. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'When a sparse point cloud is accessible... we partition the space based on the point cloud... This is achieved by recursively identifying the plane where the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) equals 0.5 for the 3D point distribution along each axis.' The claim is a direct paraphrase of the evidence provided.

The claim states that 'Partitioning runs typically within seconds'. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'This process is universally applicable to various types of captures, including street, aerial, and object-centric data, and runs very quickly in practice (typically within seconds).' Additionally, the notes for Source [S1] list 'Partitioning runs typically within seconds' as a bullet point. Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
